newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.Africa rand surges, fx control hopes rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa rand surges, fx control hopes rise.

text.p: South Africa's rand pushed to its best levels in four months on Wednesday as international funds poured back into a country shunned as the laggard among emerging markets in 1996.

The rand finished local trading at 4.4900/4930 on the dollar, a gain of 3-1/2 cents on the day. So far this year it has appreciated four percent against the greenback and over six percent on a trade-weighted basis.
Dealers and analysts said investors were being tempted back to South Africa by the high yield on rand assets and a growing consensus that the rand will stabilise this year.

Fuelling the rally was mounting speculation that President Nelson Mandela would announce bold steps to ease foreign exchange controls on residents and accelerate privatisation when he opens parliament on Friday.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel would not be drawn on exchange controls at a news conference in Cape Town, commenting only: "I've seen some very interesting rumours in the market."

South African residents are currently prevented from taking anything but small amounts of currency out the country. The government has promised to abolish restrictions eventually, in a move signalling economic confidence, but has not said when.
With the economic and political outlooking brightening, Investec economist Carole Mason said the high returns earned on holding South african assets had once more come to the fore.
"As far as yield goes, South Africa just ranks in a league of its own internationally which is why you are seeing this interest in the bond market and by extension the rand."
Foreigners have so far this year bought a net 2.41 billion rand ($535 million) of South African bonds against 635 million in the whole of the second half of 1996, according to Bond Exchange figures.
Offshore, there has been a similar dash for rand-denominated debt with Eurorand bond issues topping two billion rand in January and 650 million so far in February.

Ben Hall, South African representative of Hambros Bank, the leading issuing house for Eurorand debt, said the current rash of issues represented a sizeable inflow of new money, rather than simply rollovers of maturing bonds.

"There has been a large amount of redemption flows, which helped the market, but we have undoubtably located new money," he said, noting that new issues last month were virtually double the 1.1 billion rand of maturing debt.
Hall said investors from the Benelux countries and Italy were joining those from Germany and Switzerland in taking up Eurorands, which offer investors a coupon of around 15 percent.

Faith in South African assets has been restored by a growing belief that the rand will stabilise in 1997 and even outperform inflation differentials, which should otherwise point to a slide in the rand to over five to the dollar by the end of the year.

The outlook for the currency is seen improving on the back of a sharply improving trade balance -- with a lower rand boosting exports and curbing imports -- which in turn should boost the critically low level of foreign exchange reserves.
U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs was reported by the Financial Times on Wednesday as calculating the rand's "real value" at about 4.18 to the dollar.
Much is also riding on hopes that 1997 will be the year in which Mandela's government delivers on promises laid out in a market-orientated macroeconomic blueprint last June.

In addition to high hopes for the opening of parliament on February 7, investors also expect an upbeat budget on March 12 confirming the government is on track to cut its budget deficit, helped by privatisation receipts.
Ben van Rensburg, director of economic policy at the South African Chamber of Business, said the sharp improvement in sentiment this year gave scope for decisive action.
"There is a window of opportunity for government which it must capitalise on to strengthen the foundation from which to launch a better economy for South Africa," he said.
